sections.html: This giant, up to 2.5 metres long, is certainly no typical aquarium fish. It can reach a weight of up to 160 kg. It is euryhaline, so it can move freely from fresh to salt water and back again, and it has accessory respiration via its swimbladder, enabling it to survive in oxygen-depleted waters.

Although at first glance the tarpon resembles a clupeid, it actually has very little in common with the herring family. Its larvae are much more like those of the eels: so-called leptocephalus larvae, which resemble the elongate-oval leaves of a willow tree.

The tarpon is found on both sides of the Atlantic. The only other species in the genus, M. cyprinoides, remains significantly smaller (maximum reported length is 150 cm, but usually only 30-40 cm in the wild) and inhabits the Pacific. The specimens recently imported came from Nigeria.

In the aquarium Megalops require fish as food and can consume astonishingly large pieces. After only a few weeks they become acclimated to frozen feeder fish (smelt), which they will take from forceps.

These large predators are in no way shy and never panic in the aquarium. The observer always has the feeling that a Megalops reflects its actions and studies carefully everything that goes on outside its tank.

Megalops: from ancient Greek, means "of big appearance". atlanticus: Latin, means "deriving from the Atlantic ocean". cyprinoides: Latin, means "similar to a carp-like fish". Common names: Megalops atlanticus: Atlantic Tarpon; M. cyprinoides: Pacific Tarpon.
